title: Keyset Pagination vs. Offset Pagination: Why OFFSET 100,000 Destroys Database Performance and How Keyset Cursors Deliver Constant-Time Queries
summary: In modern web applications and distributed APIs, paginating through large collections of database records is ubiquitous. The vast majority of backend tutorials recommend the intuitive SQL construct SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000. However, in relational engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL, OFFSET does not jump directly to the 100,000th record; the database must read, sort, and process all 100,000 preceding rows off disk and memory only to discard them before returning the requested 20 records (O(N) time complexity). As pagination depth increases, queries slow from 2 milliseconds to multi-second timeouts, crushing database buffer pools and creating severe row drift when new records are inserted concurrently. Keyset pagination (also known as the Seek Method or cursor-based pagination) eliminates this bottleneck by utilizing indexed range predicates like WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_seen_created_at, :last_seen_id). By traversing directly to the target record via the B-Tree index in O(log N) time, keyset pagination guarantees rock-solid constant-time execution whether querying page 1 or page 10,000.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Blindfolded Book Flipper vs. The Precision Bookmark
analogy:
Imagine you are reading a massive 10,000-page historical encyclopedia and need to consult page 5,000.

Under Offset Pagination (OFFSET 5000), you are strictly blindfolded and forced to obey a bizarre rule: to reach page 5,000, you must open page 1 and manually count every single individual page one by one—1, 2, 3... 4,999—before you are permitted to read page 5,000. When you finish and decide to inspect page 5,001 ten minutes later, you must close the book, start back at page 1, and count all 5,001 pages from scratch! The deeper into the encyclopedia you go, the longer you spend fruitlessly counting pages you intend to throw away.

Under Keyset Pagination (WHERE page_id > 5000), you place a sleek magnetic bookmark right where you last stopped. To read the next chapter, you simply flip open the bookmark in half a second. You never visit page 1, you never count discarded pages, and reaching page 9,900 takes the exact same effortless split-second as opening page 2.

sections.heading: 1. The Myth of Fast Offsets: Why Database Engines Scan What They Discard
sections.content:
Developers frequently assume that providing an index on ORDER BY created_at allows the database engine to jump instantly to an arbitrary offset. In relational storage engines (PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB), this assumption is false:

• B-Tree Leaf Node Traversal: Standard B-Trees store keys in sorted order across linked leaf pages. However, standard B-Trees do not store cumulative subtree counts or positional ranks inside branch nodes. The engine cannot know which physical disk page holds row #100,000 without walking the chain.
• The O(N) Processing Penalty: When executing LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000, the engine scans the index, resolves 100,020 physical heap pointers, reads the tuples off disk or buffer pool, applies transaction visibility checks, throws away the first 100,000 rows, and returns the final 20. Execution time scales linearly ($O(N)$) with offset depth.
• Buffer Cache Eviction Storms: Reading 100,000 table tuples touches thousands of 8KB disk pages. This flushes active, frequently accessed data out of the shared database buffer pool, degrading cache hit ratios and slowing down unrelated application queries across the entire database instance.

sections.heading: 2. The Concurrency Nightmare: Data Drift and Ghost Duplicates
sections.content:
Beyond performance degradation, offset pagination suffers from fundamental data integrity flaws in real-time environments:

• Row Drift from Concurrent Inserts: Imagine a user loads Page 1 (rows 1 to 20). While they browse, two new records are inserted at the top of the table. When the user requests Page 2 (OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20), all existing rows have shifted down by two slots. Row #19 and Row #20 from Page 1 now appear at positions #21 and #22. The user sees duplicate rows across consecutive page views.
• Skipped Records from Concurrent Deletions: Conversely, if rows on Page 1 are deleted before Page 2 is loaded, records shift upwards, causing Page 2 to skip rows entirely without the user or client application ever realizing it.
• Stateless Instability: Offset pagination relies on an unstable temporal coordinate system that changes with every single write to the table, making it completely unsuitable for infinite scroll feeds, real-time dashboards, or distributed ETL pipelines.

sections.heading: 3. The Keyset Solution: Indexed Seek Cursors and Composite Keys
sections.content:
Keyset pagination (seek pagination) replaces offset counting with indexed range queries based on values from the last retrieved row:

• The Anchor Predicate: Instead of passing a page number, the client receives an opaque cursor containing the sorting values of the last item on the page. The next query executes: WHERE created_at < :last_created_at ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20.
• The Tie-Breaker Composite Index: In real-world databases, timestamps are not strictly unique. If multiple records share the exact same microsecond timestamp across page boundaries, simple timestamp filtering skips matching rows. To guarantee deterministic pagination, always pair the sorting attribute with a unique primary key: (created_at DESC, id DESC).
• Row-Value Syntax vs. Expanded SQL: In PostgreSQL, multi-column comparison is supported natively: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id). In MySQL or ANSI SQL, this is expressed as: WHERE (created_at < :last_created_at) OR (created_at = :last_created_at AND id < :last_id).
• Constant O(log N) Performance: With a composite B-Tree index on (created_at, id), the database engine descends the B-Tree root-to-leaf in $O(\log N)$ time, lands directly on the first valid tuple, reads exactly 20 consecutive leaf slots, and stops. Page 1,000 executes in under 1 millisecond, consuming virtually zero buffer cache.

takeaway: Using SQL OFFSET for deep pagination forces the database engine to perform costly O(N) table and index scans, evicting hot data from buffer pools and exposing client applications to data drift. Keyset pagination replaces offset counting with composite index range predicates on (timestamp, id), executing direct O(log N) B-Tree seeks that deliver stable, sub-millisecond query latencies at any depth.
